column2: Is "the long term benefit of humanity" a standard anyone can measure, or a category error?
column3: The charter's benefit names no population, metric, time scale or threshold, so no one can tell whether it is being served or when a line has been crossed; a purpose that cannot fail cannot discipline anyone, and a director can justify almost any act under it. Sloane's reading: that vagueness leaves Anthropic open to suit in the Delaware Court of Chancery. Tension to resolve: a benefit too vague to measure is also hard to prove breached, and §365(b) protects any informed, disinterested decision a person of ordinary, sound judgment could approve (statute not yet pinned); the strongest supported form may be that vagueness makes the benefit unenforceable in practice.
column4: Delaware lets a PBC name a broad benefit (DGCL §362), asks directors only to balance it (§365) and protects that balancing under the business judgment rule; breadth is what lets a long-horizon mission survive changing facts, and the five pillars give it content.

column2: What would we do if we really cared about the environment, the world and flourishing?
column3: Start from what the Earth can bear, not from what the buildout needs: set a resource budget (planetary boundaries, allocated by a stated rule), give the people who bear the effects a seat and a veto, and fit compute inside what is left.
column4: Abundance: clean energy at scale makes the budget a supply problem; AI may save more than it emits (IEA); a fixed budget freezes today's poverty.

column2: How much social harm can a society bear in return for the possibility of social gain, and who decides?
column3: A society can consent to risk for a chance of gain only if those who bear the harm have a say, can see it coming, can stop it, and are made whole; without those, it is not a trade but an imposition, and a gain that may never arrive cannot be booked against a harm that already has.
column4: Every transformative technology (electricity, aviation, medicine) imposed harm before its gains; demanding consent from everyone freezes progress, and the harms of falling behind a less careful developer are real too.

column2: Is a fixed fine a licence fee? Should penalties scale with the stakes?
column3: SB 53 caps the penalty at $1 million per violation, including for not following Anthropic's own framework. Epoch AI records Anthropic's compute spend at $13.6 billion for the first quarter of 2026: about $104,938 a minute, so one maximum fine buys about 10 minutes of compute. A penalty that small against the stakes is a price, not a deterrent: a fee for the licence to break the rule. A penalty that deters scales with the mandate, as the GDPR (a share of global turnover) and the EU AI Act already do.
column4: Where Anthropic sells in the EU, the AI Act already scales fines with turnover (for general-purpose model providers, Article 101; the exact tier is to be pinned), so a scaled penalty already applies to it; SB 53 penalties are per violation and can multiply; SB 53 also brings whistleblower protection and incident reporting, and the reputational and contractual cost of a public violation exceeds the fine; a state law that set revenue-scaled fines would invite pre-emption fights.
column5: penalty as price vs deterrent (expected cost against gain); scaling rules (share of turnover, share of compute or capex per run, per-day accrual); comparators: GDPR, EU AI Act, DMA, NRC civil penalties, FAA
